paras: The lynching of Dick Osborne took place at Ainsworth, Washington Territory, on the night of March 26-27, 1881, when a party of masked men took Osborne from the officers holding him and hanged him. Osborne, known as "Black Dick," had been arrested that day for stabbing a gambler named Alonzo Babb, who later died of his wounds. Regional papers reported that the hanging met with public approval, and a short wire carried the story to papers across the country.

Shortly before the stabbing, a committee of Ainsworth citizens appointed at a public meeting had destroyed an opium den in the town; the Walla Walla Watchman said the citizens burned it down. Osborne, described as "an opium fiend" with an interest in the den, "took exception." Accounts differ on Babb's part: the Walla Walla dispatch named him a member of the committee, while a Portland dispatch called him "merely a spectator" of the raid.

The papers described Osborne as a "rough," a "desperado" and "a hard customer" who had had "difficulties" at Boise City, Pendleton and Walla Walla, and Babb as "quiet and peaceable," with relatives at Eugene City, Oregon.

On the afternoon of Saturday, March 26, Osborne was accused of coming up behind Babb at Hill's dance-house and stabbing him three times in the back with a five-inch blade. According to the Portland dispatch, he shouted "Damn you, I'll kill you" as he struck, and one thrust pierced Babb's lung. Osborne was arrested at once and held in a small building behind the dance-house, which the Watchman called a "temporary prison"; wire versions said he was in jail.

Townspeople were "intensely excited," and threats to lynch Osborne were made openly. At about 3:15 on Sunday morning, according to the Portland dispatch, some fifteen men broke down the door, threw a rope around Osborne's neck, dragged him about thirty yards and hanged him from a high pole. The Lewiston Teller and the Watchman instead counted ten men, disguised or masked and "armed to the teeth," who demanded the prisoner from his keepers, while the wire said he was hanged from "the nearest high fence." His body was found hanging the next morning.

Babb was still alive when the first dispatch was sent; the Lewiston Teller said he died the next day, and the Sacramento Record-Union reported his death on April 4. After the hanging, a number of "roughs and desperadoes" threatened revenge on the lynchers, and the town's "orderly citizens" ordered about twenty of them to leave within half an hour. A ferryman, Capt. Smith, told the Lewiston Teller that he carried several of them across the Snake River. The coverage shows no inquest, no arrest of any of the lynchers and no official inquiry.

Papers in the Pacific Northwest generally approved of the hanging. The Portland dispatch ended, "The act seems to generally meet with public approval," and the Watchman opened its account of "The Ainsworth Tragedy" by saying the stabbing "called for hemp." A Whitman county paper, reprinted in the Daily Astorian a month later, held up the case as proof that the county would not tolerate criminals: "There was no need of a trial," and "justice reigned supreme." The Vancouver Independent was more ambivalent, writing that Osborne's "carcass was found ornamenting a pole, and the courts are cheated of the trial of a murder case."

Beyond the region the story traveled as a two-sentence wire datelined Walla Walla, run between March 28 and early April by the Chicago Tribune, the Lancaster Intelligencer, the Delaware State Journal, the Bismarck Tribune and the Helena Weekly Herald, among others. These items called Osborne "a bad character," often appeared in crime roundups such as "High Life in the West" and "Weekly Record of Crimes," and usually placed the lynching in Walla Walla itself; the McMinnville, Tennessee, Southern Standard printed the town as "Walhalla." No article gives the race of Osborne or Babb.

Beyond the place, accounts differ on the number of lynchers (about fifteen or ten) and on whether Osborne was taken from a jail or from a makeshift lockup behind the dance-house. Two wire variants also misdated the stabbing, to "Friday night" and to "the 27th."

bases: A party of ten to fifteen masked men took Dick Osborne from the officers holding him at Ainsworth, W.T., and hanged him from a fence or pole (A1, A6, A25, A26).

Osborne was hanged by masked men numbering about fifteen (A6) or ten (A25, A26) who took him from his keepers without legal authority, in punishment for his stabbing of Alonzo Babb (A1, A25); a Whitman county paper said 'There was no need of a trial' (A29).

A Walla Walla dispatch (A1, A4), a separate Portland dispatch (A6), the Lewiston Teller (A25) and the Walla Walla Watchman (A26) independently agree that Osborne stabbed Babb, was arrested and was hanged that night by masked men.

accounts.label: Walla Walla dispatch (national wire)
accounts.gist: Osborne stabbed Babb in a dance house, was arrested, and masked men broke into the jail and hanged him on the nearest high fence; the national version placed the event 'in Walla Walla'.

accounts.label: Portland dispatch
accounts.gist: Babb was only a spectator of the committee's raid; about fifteen men broke into a small building behind the dance-house at 3:15 Sunday morning and hanged Osborne from a high pole thirty yards away; the act met 'public approval'.

accounts.label: Lewiston Teller and Walla Walla Watchman
accounts.gist: Ten disguised or masked men demanded Osborne from his keepers at a temporary prison and hanged him; roughs who threatened revenge were driven out of town.

framing.detail: Pacific Northwest papers called Osborne a 'desperado' and 'hard customer', Babb 'quiet and peaceable', and reported that the hanging 'seems to generally meet with public approval' and that 'justice reigned supreme'.
The Vancouver Independent wrote flippantly of the 'carcass' 'ornamenting a pole' while noting 'the courts are cheated of the trial of a murder case'.
Eastern and Midwestern papers ran a two-sentence wire, often in crime roundups such as 'High Life in the West' or 'Weekly Record of Crimes', calling Osborne 'a bad character'.

conflicts.note: The Walla Walla dispatch itself says 'At Ainsworth'; papers that shortened the wire turned its dateline into the scene. Ainsworth is supported by every detailed and regional account.
The Walla Walla dispatch of March 27 and the Lewiston Teller agree on the 26th.
Compatible: the same night, after midnight.
